analogy.p: Imagine a library that wants to split into two identical libraries. First the library grows its building and stock of shelves (cell growth). Then it photocopies every book (DNA replication). Then one complete copy of every book is carried to each end of the building (mitosis), and a wall is built down the middle (cytokinesis). Each new library has a full set of books and all the equipment it needs. The analogy breaks down because books do not have a mistake-prone copying process like DNA, and real cells make the equipment as well as the books.
analogy.t: Photocopying a book and making two libraries

bullets: The **nucleus** contains the **chromosomes**; it is surrounded by a nuclear membrane (envelope) with pores.
A **chromosome** is made of one **DNA molecule**, wrapped around proteins and coiled up.
**DNA** carries the genetic code; it is a double helix (two strands wound together) and is described in more detail in the inheritance topic.
Prokaryotic cells such as bacteria have **no nucleus**; their DNA is a single loop free in the cytoplasm, so they do not use mitosis.
Chromosomes can only be seen as separate structures with a light microscope when the cell is about to divide; at other times they are spread out as fine threads.
Link to other topics: the **genome** is the entire genetic material of an organism, and the sequence of bases along DNA decides the order of amino acids in proteins.
core.h: Where the genetic material is kept
core.p: In a eukaryotic cell (animals, plants, fungi and protists) the genetic material is stored in the **nucleus**. It is organised into long, thread-like structures called **chromosomes**. Each chromosome is a single, very long molecule of **DNA** that has been coiled up tightly so it fits inside the tiny nucleus. The nucleus acts as the control centre of the cell because the DNA holds the instructions for making every protein the cell needs.

bullets: A **gene** = a small section of DNA on a chromosome that codes for a particular sequence of amino acids, i.e. a specific protein.
Each chromosome carries **a large number of genes** (human chromosomes carry hundreds to thousands).
Different forms of the same gene are called **alleles**; they are found at the same position on matching chromosomes (link to inheritance).
Proteins made from genes decide a cell's structure and function, so genes help determine the characteristics of the organism.
The genes on a chromosome are copied together when the chromosome is copied, so all the genes are passed on in mitosis.
Only part of a cell's genes are active in any particular cell type, which is why different cells can have the same genes but look different (link to differentiation).
core.p: Each chromosome carries a very large number of **genes**. A gene is a short section of DNA that codes for a particular **protein**, so it controls a characteristic such as eye colour or the production of an enzyme. Genes are arranged one after another along the length of the chromosome, and each gene always sits at the same position (locus) on its chromosome. A chromosome can therefore be thought of as a long instruction manual, with each gene being one instruction.

bullets: Body (somatic) cells have chromosomes in **pairs**: this is called the **diploid** number (2n).
Humans have **23 pairs = 46 chromosomes** in each normal body cell.
22 of the pairs control general characteristics; the 23rd pair carries the genes that determine sex (XX in females, XY in males).
The two chromosomes in a pair are the same length and carry genes for the same characteristics in the same order.
Gametes (sex cells: egg and sperm) have only one chromosome from each pair - 23 chromosomes - the **haploid** number, produced by meiosis (a different division).
When egg and sperm join at fertilisation the pairs are restored, giving the new cell 46 chromosomes.
Different species have different numbers of chromosomes; the number is characteristic of the species.
core.p: In **body cells** the chromosomes are normally found in **pairs**. One chromosome in each pair came from the mother and the other from the father. The two chromosomes of a pair are the same size and carry the same genes (although they may carry different alleles of those genes). Human body cells have **23 pairs** of chromosomes, giving a total of **46 chromosomes**.

bullets: The cell cycle is a **series of stages** that a cell goes through between one division and the next.
**Stage 1 - growth:** the cell grows and increases the number of **sub-cellular structures** such as ribosomes and mitochondria.
**Stage 2 - DNA replication:** the **DNA replicates** to form two copies of each chromosome.
**Stage 3 - mitosis:** one set of chromosomes is pulled to each end of the cell and the **nucleus divides**.
**Stage 4 - cytokinesis:** the **cytoplasm and cell membranes divide** to form two identical cells.
Stages 1 and 2 together make up **interphase**, which is the longest part of the cycle.
The two new cells can go round the cycle again, which is how a single cell can give rise to millions of cells.
Not every cell in the body keeps dividing: many specialised cells have stopped and no longer go through the cycle.
core.p: Cells divide in a series of stages called the **cell cycle**. The cycle begins with the cell growing and getting ready to divide, continues with the doubling of the genetic material, then the nucleus divides (**mitosis**), and finally the whole cell divides in two. The cycle then starts again in each new cell. The long period of growth and preparation between divisions is called **interphase**, and the actual division is much shorter.

bullets: Increasing the number of **ribosomes** means each daughter cell can make proteins.
Increasing the number of **mitochondria** means each daughter cell can release energy by aerobic respiration.
Other organelles (and the cytoplasm) are also increased so each new cell is complete.
**DNA replication** makes each chromosome into two identical copies, joined together at a point called the centromere; each copy is a **chromatid**.
Because DNA is copied exactly, each new cell gets the same genetic information as the parent cell.
Rare copying mistakes are **mutations**; they can change genes and, in some cases, cause problems such as cancer (link to inheritance).
The energy for growth and replication comes from **respiration** in the mitochondria.
core.h: Why the cell grows and copies its DNA first
core.p: Before a cell divides, it has to prepare. If a cell divided without growing, the daughter cells would each be half the size and would not have enough cell contents to survive. Cells therefore **grow** and make more of their **sub-cellular structures** so that each new cell receives its own set. The cell must also make an exact copy of its DNA so that each daughter cell has a complete set of genetic instructions.

bullets: Early stage (prophase): chromosomes coil up and become shorter and thicker, so they become visible; the nuclear membrane breaks down.
Chromosomes line up across the middle of the cell (metaphase), attached to fibres called the spindle.
The spindle fibres pull the two chromatids of each chromosome apart (anaphase), so one set of chromosomes moves towards each end of the cell.
A new nuclear membrane forms around each set of chromosomes (telophase), giving two nuclei.
After mitosis, each nucleus holds the **same number and type of chromosomes** as the original (46 in a human cell).
The two sets of chromosomes are **genetically identical** because they came from the same copied DNA.
Mitosis is the division of the **nucleus** only; the division of the rest of the cell is a separate step.
core.p: In mitosis the nucleus divides so that each daughter nucleus receives one complete copy of every chromosome. Before mitosis the chromosomes have already been copied, so each chromosome consists of two identical **chromatids**. During mitosis **one set of chromosomes is pulled to each end of the cell** and the nucleus divides. The AQA specification does not require the names of the sub-stages, but they help to understand the process and are needed by some other exam boards.

bullets: Cytoplasm and cell membrane divide **after** the nucleus has divided.
The result is **two daughter cells** that are genetically identical to each other and to the parent cell.
Each daughter cell is **diploid**: it has the same chromosome number as the parent (46 in humans).
Daughter cells are initially smaller than the parent cell and need to grow before dividing again.
In plants a **cell wall** forms between the new cells.
Mitosis produces **clones** at the cell level: no new genetic variation is made (unlike meiosis).
core.p: Once the two new nuclei have formed, the rest of the cell divides. The **cytoplasm** and the **cell membranes** divide to form **two identical cells**. Each daughter cell has a nucleus and a share of the ribosomes, mitochondria and other organelles that were made earlier in the cycle. In plant cells a new cell wall also forms between the daughter cells. The daughter cells are now ready to carry out their jobs or to go round the cell cycle again.

bullets: **Growth:** a zygote becomes an embryo then an adult by repeated mitosis, increasing the number of cells.
**Development:** new cells produced by mitosis can then differentiate into specialised cells (link to cell differentiation and stem cells).
**Repair and replacement:** skin cells, gut lining cells and blood cells are replaced by mitosis; wounds heal by mitosis.
**Asexual reproduction:** some organisms produce genetically identical offspring (clones) by mitosis, e.g. strawberry runners, bacteria divide by binary fission (a different but similar process).
All the cells produced have the **same genes**, so they are genetically identical to the parent cell.
Mitosis keeps the chromosome number the same, so the organism does not double its chromosomes each time.
Uncontrolled mitosis causes **cancer**, where cells divide too often and form a lump called a tumour (link to non-communicable disease).
core.p: Cell division by mitosis is important in the **growth and development** of multicellular organisms. A fertilised egg is a single cell, and mitosis produces all the cells of the body. Mitosis also **repairs** damaged tissue and replaces worn-out cells, and in some organisms it is the basis of **asexual reproduction**. In every case, the cells produced must have exactly the same genetic information, which is why mitosis suits these jobs.

bullets: Mitosis makes **two** cells; meiosis makes **four**.
Mitosis daughter cells are **genetically identical**; meiosis cells are all **genetically different**.
Mitosis keeps the chromosome number the same (**46 to 46**); meiosis halves it (**46 to 23**).
Mitosis occurs in body cells for growth and repair; meiosis occurs only in the reproductive organs to make gametes.
Mitosis involves one division; meiosis involves two divisions.
Mitosis is part of the cell cycle that produces clones; meiosis produces variation.
core.p: It helps to know how mitosis differs from the type of division that makes gametes (meiosis, covered under inheritance). The two processes have different jobs, so they produce different results. This comparison is often asked in exam questions.

bullets: Cells after n divisions = starting cells x 2^n (one cell: 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64 ...).
A copied chromosome has **2 chromatids**, so a human cell after DNA replication has 46 chromosomes but **92 chromatids**.
After mitosis each daughter cell has **46 chromosomes** (each chromosome has only one chromatid again).
Time to produce a number of cells = number of divisions x time for one cell cycle.
To find the number of divisions needed for a target number of cells, find the power of 2 that reaches it: 2^10 = 1024.
Percentage of cells in mitosis (from a microscope count) = cells in mitosis / total cells x 100; use this to estimate how fast tissue is dividing.
core.h: Calculating cell numbers and chromosome counts
core.p: Mitosis questions often include simple calculations. Each division doubles the number of cells, so after n divisions one cell becomes 2^n cells. Chromosome questions test whether you know that DNA is copied before the cell divides and that each daughter cell receives a full set. Be careful about the difference between the number of chromosomes and the number of chromatids.

bullets: Replication makes an identical copy of the DNA molecule in each chromosome.
The original and the copy are called sister chromatids and stay joined at the centromere.
Count chromosomes by the number of centromeres, not by the number of arms.
Before replication: 46 chromosomes, each one chromatid.
After replication: 46 chromosomes, each with two chromatids (92 chromatids).
After the chromatids separate: 92 chromosomes in the dividing cell, 46 going to each end.
Each daughter cell therefore ends with 46 single chromosomes.
The cell must replicate DNA before mitosis so that both daughter cells can receive a full set.
core.p: When DNA replicates, each chromosome is copied so that it consists of two identical chromatids joined at a region called the centromere. The two chromatids carry exactly the same genes in the same order because one is an exact copy of the other. The cell still counts this as one chromosome, so 46 chromosomes become 46 chromosomes each made of two chromatids, which is 92 chromatids in total. During mitosis the chromatids are pulled apart and each one then counts as a chromosome in its own right.

bullets: Growth: a fertilised egg divides repeatedly by mitosis to form an embryo and then the whole body.
Repair: damaged skin or tissue is replaced by new cells made by mitosis.
Replacement: cells such as skin and gut lining are constantly lost and remade.
Plants: meristems at root and shoot tips contain cells that keep dividing by mitosis.
Asexual reproduction: single-celled organisms and some plants and animals produce genetically identical offspring by mitosis.
Mitosis is not used to make gametes; that is meiosis.
Cells made by mitosis may later differentiate, but they start genetically identical.
Link to stem cells: embryonic stem cells and meristem cells divide by mitosis and can differentiate.
core.p: Mitosis happens wherever an organism needs more body cells or replacement cells. In animals this includes the skin, the lining of the gut and the bone marrow, where cells are lost or damaged all the time, and in a growing embryo where it makes the cells needed for development. In plants, mitosis occurs mainly in regions called meristems at the tips of roots and shoots, which allows the plant to grow in length. The new cells are then able to differentiate into the specialised cell types that the organism needs.

bullets: Normal cell division is controlled; cancer cells divide uncontrollably.
A tumour is a mass of abnormal cells.
Benign tumours grow in one place and do not invade other tissues.
Malignant tumours invade neighbouring tissue and spread, forming secondary tumours; these are cancers.
Cancer starts with changes (mutations) in DNA in a cell.
Some risk factors include smoking, UV radiation and certain viruses, and some genes inherited from parents.
Uncontrolled mitosis is a good example of why the controlled cell cycle matters.
Exam link: explain that cancer is caused by uncontrolled cell division.
core.h: When the control of cell division fails
core.p: In a healthy body the rate of cell division is controlled so that the right number of cells is produced. Changes (mutations) in the DNA of a cell can stop this control, so that the cell divides again and again by mitosis in an uncontrolled way. The mass of abnormal cells that forms is a tumour. Cancer is the result of such changes that lead to uncontrolled growth and division, and malignant tumour cells can invade neighbouring tissues and spread to other parts of the body.

bullets: Use the sequence: growth, replication, mitosis, cytokinesis.
Use the term genetically identical for the two daughter cells.
State chromosome numbers for each stage when asked.
In a drawing, the chromosomes should be pulled to opposite ends before the cell splits.
Label the nucleus, cell membrane, cytoplasm and chromosomes using a ruler for label lines.
Explain steps with because or so that: DNA replicates so each daughter cell gets a full set.
Do not call mitosis the whole cell cycle.
Do not mix up mitosis with meiosis: mitosis gives 2 identical cells, meiosis gives 4 different cells.
core.h: Describing and drawing mitosis in the exam
core.p: Examination questions on mitosis usually ask you to describe the order of events, to explain why a step is needed or to complete a diagram. Always keep the sequence in mind: the cell grows and copies its DNA, one set of chromosomes is pulled to each end, the nucleus divides, and then the cytoplasm and membrane divide. When you draw or complete diagrams, check that each daughter cell has the same number of chromosomes as the parent and that the chromosomes are shown as copies lined up in the middle before they are pulled apart.

exam: **Describe the cell cycle (4 marks):** (1) cell grows and makes more ribosomes/mitochondria; (2) DNA replicates to form two copies of each chromosome; (3) mitosis - one set of chromosomes pulled to each end and the nucleus divides; (4) cytoplasm and cell membranes divide to form two identical cells.
**Why does the cell make more mitochondria and ribosomes before dividing? (2 marks):** so each daughter cell has enough of these structures (1) to release energy / make proteins (1).
**Why must DNA replicate before mitosis? (2 marks):** so each daughter cell receives a full set of chromosomes / identical genetic information (2).
**Importance of mitosis (2-3 marks):** growth and development of multicellular organisms; repair/replacement of damaged cells; asexual reproduction. Always link to genetically identical cells.
**Chromosome number questions:** Parent 46 -> after replication 46 chromosomes (92 chromatids) -> each daughter 46. State the number for each stage.
**Compare mitosis and meiosis (3-4 marks):** number of cells (2 v 4), genetic makeup (identical v different), chromosome number (46 v 23), where it happens.
**Cell number calculations:** write cells = 2^n and show n; check by doubling one step at a time.
**Command words:** 'describe' = what happens in order; 'explain' = give a reason using 'because/so that'; 'state' = one short fact.
**Diagrams:** if shown cells in mitosis, check the chromosome number is the same in each daughter cell; label nucleus, chromosomes, cell membrane.
**Terminology:** use 'chromosomes' for the DNA structures, 'genes' for sections, 'genetically identical' for the product, not 'the same' or 'clones' alone.
**Cancer link (2 marks):** cancer is caused by uncontrolled cell division (1) by mitosis forming a tumour (1).

mistakes.r: Mitosis produces two daughter cells that are genetically identical to each other and to the parent cell.
mistakes.w: Mitosis makes four cells that are all different.

mistakes.r: The chromosome number stays the same in mitosis (46 in a human cell); halving happens in meiosis.
mistakes.w: The chromosome number is halved in mitosis.

mistakes.r: DNA is replicated before the cell divides, so that each daughter cell receives a full set of chromosomes.
mistakes.w: The cell divides first and then copies its DNA.

mistakes.r: Mitosis is the stage where the nucleus divides; the cell cycle also includes cell growth, DNA replication and division of the cytoplasm.
mistakes.w: Mitosis is the whole cell cycle.

mistakes.r: A chromosome is a long DNA molecule that carries many genes; a gene is a short section of a chromosome coding for a protein.
mistakes.w: Genes and chromosomes are the same thing.

mistakes.r: Human body cells have 23 pairs = 46 chromosomes; gametes have 23.
Mitosis happens in the nucleus; the cell first makes more ribosomes and mitochondria so each new cell has some.
mistakes.w: Mitosis happens in the ribosomes / mitochondria.

mistakes.r: Cells are genetically identical because they contain exactly the same DNA.
mistakes.w: The cells are identical because they are the same size.

mistakes.r: Gametes are made by meiosis; mitosis is used for growth, repair and asexual reproduction.
mistakes.w: Mitosis is used to make gametes.

mistakes.r: The copies stay joined as chromatids, so there are still 46 chromosomes (92 chromatids) until the chromatids separate.
mistakes.w: Once DNA is copied there are 92 chromosomes.

summary: You must know that the nucleus of a eukaryotic cell contains chromosomes made of DNA, each carrying many genes and normally found in pairs, and that cells divide by mitosis as part of the cell cycle: the genetic material is doubled, one set of chromosomes is pulled to each end, the nucleus divides, then the cytoplasm and membrane divide to give two identical cells. This explains how organisms grow, develop and repair themselves, and it underpins later topics such as stem cells, cancer and asexual reproduction.

terms.d: The part of a eukaryotic cell that contains the genetic material in the form of chromosomes.
A long molecule of DNA, coiled up, found in the nucleus; it carries a large number of genes.
A small section of DNA on a chromosome that codes for a particular protein.
Deoxyribonucleic acid, the molecule that carries the genetic code.
Two chromosomes of the same size carrying the same genes, one from each parent; body cells normally have chromosomes in pairs.
A cell with two sets of chromosomes (pairs); human body cells have 46.
A cell with one set of chromosomes; human gametes have 23.
A series of stages that a cell goes through in order to divide, in which the genetic material is doubled and then divided into two identical cells.
The stage of the cell cycle when the cell grows, increases the number of sub-cellular structures and replicates its DNA.
The copying of DNA to form two identical copies of each chromosome.
One of the two identical copies of a replicated chromosome, joined at the centromere.
Cell division in which one set of chromosomes is pulled to each end of the cell and the nucleus divides, producing genetically identical nuclei.
The division of the cytoplasm and cell membrane to form two cells after mitosis.
One of the new cells produced when a cell divides.
Having exactly the same genes (the same DNA); clones.
A component within a cell, such as a ribosome or mitochondrion.
Reproduction involving one parent and mitosis, producing offspring that are genetically identical to the parent.
A mass of cells produced by uncontrolled cell division.
The region where the two chromatids of a copied chromosome are joined.
A region of plant tissue, such as at root and shoot tips, where cells divide by mitosis.

worked.ans: (a) 46 chromosomes (92 chromatids); (b) 46 chromosomes in each daughter cell
worked.q: A human skin cell has 46 chromosomes. State how many chromosomes there are in (a) the cell just after DNA replication and (b) each daughter cell after mitosis and cytokinesis. (2 marks)
steps: Replication copies each chromosome, but the copies stay joined as chromatids, so the number of chromosomes is still 46 (92 chromatids).
Mitosis pulls one copy of each chromosome to each end, so each nucleus has 46 chromosomes.

worked.q: A single cell divides by mitosis every 24 hours. How many cells will there be after 6 days? (2 marks)

worked.ans: Model answer: The cell grows and makes more ribosomes and mitochondria. DNA replicates so there are two copies of each chromosome. In mitosis one set of chromosomes is pulled to each end of the cell and the nucleus divides. Then the cytoplasm and cell membrane divide to form two identical daughter cells with the same number of chromosomes as the parent.
worked.q: Describe what happens to the chromosomes and the cell during the cell cycle ending in mitosis. (4 marks)
steps: Before dividing the cell grows and increases the number of sub-cellular structures such as ribosomes and mitochondria.
The DNA replicates to form two copies of each chromosome.
In mitosis one set of chromosomes is pulled to each end of the cell and the nucleus divides.
The cytoplasm and cell membranes divide to form two genetically identical cells.
